newsitem.title: UK: British royals sink in poll, tabloids undeterred.
newsitem.headline: British royals sink in poll, tabloids undeterred.

text.p: Britain's troubled royal family appeared to hit a new low on Tuesday when an opinion poll showed public support for the monarchy sinking below 50 percent for the first time.
But the antics of the tabloid press suggest that same public retains a near insatiable appetite for all scandals rich and royal, particularly when Princess Diana is concerned.
An ICM poll published in the Guardian newspaper on Tuesday showed only 48 percent of Britons felt the country would be worse off without the royal family.
Just three years -- and many scandals -- earlier, that figure towered at 70 percent.
The odds on the monarchy being abolished by the year 2020 were slashed from 100-1 to 33-1 by bookmakers William Hill on Tuesday after the poll was released.
The royal family has repeatedly stumbled in the public's eyes in recent years over a spate of divorces and glaring admissions of affairs by Diana and former husband Prince Charles.

But this has not sated the appetite of the royalty-obsessed tabloids, which at the moment simply cannot get enough of Diana and what seems to be her new romance with jet-setting film producer Dodi Fayed.
Their saga has been splashed across front pages since last week, with British papers paying nearly 700,000 pounds ($1.1 million) for several grainy paparazzi shots of the pair.

But the public seems to approve of Diana's attempts to build a personal life free from royal constraints. A poll published in the Sun tabloid showed 69 percent of people felt she should be free to choose her own friends without concern of how they reflect on the royal family.
Fayed is the son of the controversial owner of the opulent Harrods department store, Mohammed Al Fayed, who has twice been denied British citizenship.

Another poll conducted by NOP Research Group showed three-quarters of Britons do not want Diana to leave the country and live abroad to escape media attention, something she has been quoted as saying her children want her to do.
Her approval rating in the NOP poll stood at nearly 50 percent, whereas Camilla Parker-Bowles, long-time mistress of Prince Charles, received just 14 percent.

The House of Windsor might take heart from the fact that only 30 percent of those polled by ICM believed Britain would be better off without the monarchy although that was more than a decade ago, when it was 10 percent.
The elder generations remained a loyal bulwark of support, with the over 65s being the only group to produce a clear majority that believed Britain would be worse off without royalty.

While more than three quarters of those polled in the Guardian rejected the idea of Parker-Bowles becoming queen, Charles has gained favour with the public as the successor to his mother, Queen Elizabeth.
Fifty-five percent said he should take the throne compared with 44 percent a year ago. ($ = 0.632 British Pounds)
